name: Big O Notation
intent: Describe how the cost of code (steps, memory) grows as its input grows, so you can tell a function that will survive 10 times more data from one that will not, without running it.
scenario: An order service checks a list of order ids for duplicates. The first version compares every pair of ids. It is instant on a test list of 10 ids, fine at 1,000, painful at 100,000 and unusable at 5,000,000. A version that remembers ids it has seen stays fast at every size, until someone gives it a heavy per-item cost and it loses at small sizes.
problem: A function that runs well on the data in your laptop tells you little about the data in production. Two pieces of code that both take a millisecond today can differ by a factor of a million next year. Timing alone cannot say which one will fall over, because the slow one only reveals itself when the input grows. Without a shared vocabulary for growth, a review comment such as "this looks slow" cannot be argued about, and the accidental quadratic loop ships.

howItWorks.title: Measure growth, not speed
howItWorks.text: Big O describes how the number of steps grows with the size of the input, n. A step is whatever you decide to count: a comparison, an element visited, a copy. It deliberately ignores how fast the machine is. Doubling n and seeing what happens to the cost is the whole idea: O(n) doubles, O(n²) quadruples, O(log n) adds one step.

howItWorks.title: Drop constants and lower-order terms
howItWorks.text: 5n + 200 and n are both O(n), and n² + 1,000n is O(n²): only the term that dominates for large n is kept, because it decides the shape of the curve. This is what makes Big O easy to state, and also what it hides: a constant factor of 100 is real time on the clock, and a lower-order term can dominate at the sizes you actually run.

howItWorks.title: Learn the common classes in order
howItWorks.text: From cheapest to most expensive: O(1) constant (array index, hash lookup on average), O(log n) (binary search: halve the range each step), O(n) (one pass), O(n log n) (good comparison sorts), O(n²) (every pair), O(2ⁿ) (every subset), O(n!) (every ordering). The first five are usable at millions of items. The last two stop being usable at tiny sizes (O(n!) around n = 15, O(2ⁿ) somewhere between n = 30 and n = 50), whatever the hardware.

howItWorks.title: Read the code for its shape
howItWorks.text: One loop over n items is O(n). A loop inside a loop over the same data is O(n²). A loop that halves the remaining range each time (binary search) is O(log n). Two loops one after the other add (O(n) + O(n) is still O(n)), while nested loops multiply. Recursion that makes two calls on a problem one smaller is O(2ⁿ); recursion that splits in half and does a pass over everything at each level is O(n log n). Also count what the calls inside the loop cost: a loop of n iterations that calls an O(n) function is O(n²).

howItWorks.title: Say which case, and which n
howItWorks.text: The same code has a best, average and worst case: linear search finds the target at once (1 step) or only at the end (n steps). Say which one you mean. When the cost depends on two inputs, keep both: comparing every item of a list of a items with every item of a list of b items is O(a·b), and scanning both once is O(a + b). Use O(n) for something that depends on two sizes and you lose the information that matters.

pros: A shared way to compare designs before running anything, and to predict what 10 or 1,000 times more data does
Independent of the machine, the language and the day's load, so a conclusion survives a hardware change
Quickly rules out the classes that cannot work at your scale: O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) at anything beyond tiny inputs, O(n²) at millions of items
Gives reviews and design discussions something precise to argue about
cons: Throws away constants, so it cannot say which of two algorithms in the same class is faster, or whether O(n log n) with a big constant beats O(n²) at your size
Describes growth for large n, so it can mislead for the small inputs most code actually sees
Counts one kind of step; memory use, cache behaviour, disk and network round trips are different costs that need their own analysis
An upper bound is not a prediction: it says the cost will not grow faster than that, not how long it takes
whenToUse: Choosing between data structures or algorithms before the input size is known
Reviewing code that loops over data that will grow: users, rows, events, files
Explaining why something fell over at scale, or estimating whether it will
whenNotToUse: As the only measure when the input is always small and bounded: for a list of 20 items, readability matters more than the class
To pick between two algorithms of the same class, or between classes that are close at your size: measure instead (see profiling)
For costs Big O does not count, such as a network call per item, memory pressure or lock contention, unless you count those as the steps
pitfalls: Believing O(1) means fast: it means the cost does not grow with n, and the constant can be large (hashing a long key is O(1) in the number of entries and still slow)
Dropping the constant and forgetting it exists: an O(n) algorithm that does 100 times the work per item loses to a plain O(n²) one until n passes 100
Treating O(n²) as always bad: for n = 50 it is 2,500 steps and fine, for n = 5,000,000 it is about 12.5 trillion and the job never finishes
Reading Big O as a time prediction: it is an upper bound on growth, not the number of milliseconds
Using one n for code with two inputs: matching a items against b items is O(a·b), not O(n²), and one of them may be tiny
Mixing up Big O with worst case: Big O is a bound on a function, and you can state one for the best, average or worst case. "The worst case is O(n)" is a complete sentence, "it is O(n)" is not
Counting a loop and missing what the body calls: an innocent-looking list lookup or string copy inside the loop turns O(n) into O(n²)
Calling something O(n log n) because it sorts, when the sort sits inside a loop and the real cost is O(n² log n)

quiz.question: A function that is O(n²) takes 2 seconds on 1,000 items. Roughly how long should it take on 10,000 items?
options: About 4 seconds, since the input is 10 times larger.
About 20 seconds, the 10 times larger input costing 10 times more.
About 200 seconds, since 10 times the input is 100 times the steps.
About 2,000 seconds, because the cost grows with the cube of n.
quiz.explanation: Quadratic cost grows with the square of n: 10 times the items is 10 x 10 = 100 times the steps, so 2 s becomes about 200 s. The prediction is only as good as the model (constants and caches shift it), but the factor 100 is what Big O tells you.

quiz.question: Function A is O(1) and function B is O(n). Called with a list of 10 items, can B be faster than A?
options: No, because a constant cost is always lower than a cost that grows.
No, because Big O orders algorithms by speed at every input size.
Only if B were really O(log n), since O(n) can never beat a constant.
Yes, because O(1) hides a constant, and A's constant may be larger than 10 steps.
quiz.explanation: O(1) means the cost does not depend on n, not that it is small. If A does 500 steps every time and B does one step per item, B wins at n = 10. Big O says who wins as n grows, not at one particular n.

quiz.question: Linear search over an unsorted list finds the target in the first position in the best case. Which statement is correct?
options: Its Big O is O(1), because Big O always describes the best case.
Its best case is O(1) and its worst case is O(n), so name the case.
Its Big O is O(n), and a best case cannot be stated in Big O at all.
Its average case is O(1), since the target is usually found early.
quiz.explanation: Big O is a bound on growth and can describe any case. Linear search is O(1) in the best case, about n/2 steps on average when the target is present (still O(n)) and O(n) in the worst case. Saying only "it is O(n)" usually means the worst case, so say so.
